summary: This informational memo documents the parameters used in MAPOS version 1, the Multiple Access Protocol over SONET/SDH.

plainLanguage.summary: A reference list of the numbers and values the MAPOS rules use.

questions: what is the mapos ipv4 protocol number
subtitle: The registry of Protocol field values used by MAPOS version 1, a multiple-access link layer for SONET/SDH.

tldr.problem: MAPOS version 1 frames carry a 16-bit Protocol field, and everyone using the protocol needs the same list of which values mean what.
tldr.mechanism: This memo lists the assigned Protocol values, such as 0021 for IPv4 and FE01 for ARP, and sets a rule on the least significant bit of each octet.
tldr.outcome: It is a short reference for implementers of MAPOS version 1. It is not a standards-track document and is not an IETF working group product.

today: RFC 2172 is an Informational memo, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The protocol itself is defined in RFC 2171.

sections.title: What MAPOS Is
sections.content:
MAPOS (Multiple Access Protocol over SONET/SDH) is a high-speed link-layer protocol that provides multiple access over SONET/SDH links. Its frame format is based on the HDLC-like framing used for PPP. A component called a Frame Switch lets multiple nodes connect in a star topology to form a LAN, which can span a wide area over long-haul SONET/SDH links. IP datagrams are sent in MAPOS HDLC frames.

The authors' note states that this document is not the product of an IETF working group, is not standards track, and has not necessarily had the in-depth community review that standards-track documents get.
sections.plainLanguage: MAPOS lets many computers share a fast fiber-optic line, a bit like many houses on one street. This note is only about the numbers it uses.

sections.title: The Protocol Field Rule
sections.content: The MAPOS version 1 data link layer has a 16-bit Protocol field that identifies the encapsulated protocol. It follows the ISO 3309 (HDLC) extension mechanism for address fields. Every protocol number MUST be assigned so that the least significant bit of the most significant octet is 0 and the least significant bit of the least significant octet is 1.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a rule about the first and last tiny bits of every number, so receivers can tell where one number ends.

sections.title: Assigned Protocol Numbers
sections.content: The memo lists four assigned values, in hexadecimal: 0021 for IPv4 (defined in RFC 2176), FE01 for the Address Resolution Protocol, FE03 for the Node Switch Protocol (RFC 2173) and FE05 for the Switch Switch Protocol (RFC 2174). The ranges 0001-001F, 0023-FCFF and FE07-FEFF are marked as not used and reserved.
sections.plainLanguage: A few numbers are already taken for internet mail, address lookup, and two jobs the switches do. The rest are saved for later.
